drills.q: True or false: in Rust, assignment always copies the value being assigned.
drills.a: False -- assignment moves by default for non-Copy types (like String or Vec<T>); only types implementing the Copy marker trait (pure stack data with no Drop impl) are bit-copied on assignment.

drills.q: Can a type that implements Drop also implement Copy?
drills.a: No -- Copy requires a bit-for-bit duplicate to be safe, but a custom Drop implementation means there's a resource/cleanup action that would run twice on two 'copies', which is unsound. The compiler rejects this combination.

drills.q: What Rust edition introduced Non-Lexical Lifetimes (NLL)?

A function holds a &Vec<T> shared reference and then tries to push() to the same Vec through a separate &mut Vec<T> in the same scope, with the shared reference still used afterward. Does this compile, and why or why not?
drills.a: No -- the borrow checker rejects it because the shared reference is still live (used later) when the mutable borrow is attempted, and push() could reallocate the Vec's backing buffer, which would invalidate the shared reference. This is exactly the aliasing-plus-mutation bug class the borrow rule prevents.

drills.q: Explain why a String parameter taken by value (fn f(s: String)) forces the caller to either move or clone their String, and when that's the right API choice.
drills.a: Taking String by value means f takes ownership -- the caller's binding becomes invalid after the call unless they clone first. It's the right choice when f genuinely needs to own, store, or consume the data (e.g. building a struct that holds it); for read-only access, &str is the correct, more flexible parameter type.

drills.q: Why does thread::spawn require captured data to be 'static, and what's the usually-correct fix when this error appears?
drills.a: A spawned thread may outlive the stack frame that created it, so any borrowed data it captures could become dangling. The usually-correct fix is to move an owned value into the closure (so no borrow, and thus no lifetime constraint, exists) rather than reaching for Box::leak to manufacture a 'static reference.

drills.q: What are the three standard escape hatches for implementing a doubly-linked list (or any back-pointer/graph shape) in Rust, and what's the real cost of each?
drills.a: Rc<RefCell<Node>> (shared ownership + interior mutability; refcounting overhead, reference cycles can leak memory since Rc alone doesn't collect cycles); arena + usize indices instead of pointers (sidesteps the borrow checker entirely, usually the fastest and used by libraries like petgraph); unsafe raw pointers with manually-upheld invariants (what the standard library's own LinkedList does internally).

drills.q: Explain the connection between the borrow checker's single-thread aliasing rule and Rust's compile-time data-race freedom across threads.
drills.a: A data race is unsynchronized concurrent memory access where at least one access writes -- exactly what the borrow rule (no &mut T alongside any other live reference) already forbids within one thread. Extending this guarantee across threads requires the Send and Sync marker traits, which certify a type is actually safe to transfer or share between threads; combined, the type system statically rejects data races for all safe Rust code, a guarantee no mainstream garbage-collected language provides.

drills.q: A codebase has .clone() calls scattered across nearly every function that touches a shared data structure, and profiling shows meaningful time in allocation. Diagnose and propose a fix.
drills.a: This is the classic 'fought the borrow checker with clone() instead of restructuring ownership' anti-pattern -- each clone is a real O(n) heap allocation and byte copy, not free. Fix by identifying which call sites genuinely need an owned, independent copy (keep those) versus which only need read-only or temporarily-exclusive access (convert to & or &mut references), and consider Rc/Arc deliberately for the cases that do need genuine shared ownership rather than repeated cloning.

drills.q: What does Box<dyn Trait> default to in terms of lifetime, and when does this surprise people?
drills.a: It defaults to Box<dyn Trait + 'static>, meaning the boxed value must not internally borrow anything with a lifetime shorter than 'static. This surprises people trying to box a trait object that holds a borrowed reference internally -- it requires an explicit Box<dyn Trait + 'a> annotation instead of the default.
